# Interlude — The Rules of Evidence

**Read after Lab 0, before Lab 1** · no Factorio required · ~20 minutes

Lab 0 handed you one machine and asked for three numbers: what's inside,
what entered, what left. Small as it was, every measurement discipline
this course enforces was already present. This interlude names the rules
you were following — because from here on the systems grow, and the rules
are what keep large numbers from becoming large lies.

## A number is a claim with a method

Every figure a FISL report prints carries three attachments: the
**method** that produced it, the **window** it was measured over, and a
**validity** verdict. This is not decoration. "Throughput 15/min" is not
a fact; "15 completions per minute across the sink boundary, over the
10-minute measured window, census clean" is. Strip the attachments and
two honest numbers become incomparable — or worse, comparable-looking.

The habit to build now: whenever you see a rate or a fraction, ask *per
what?* A rate is a count divided by a window; a fraction is a count
divided by a denominator. Both halves are choices, and both halves can
be wrong independently of the count.

## The boundary is declared, not discovered

Lab 0's blue and orange ports were not scenery: they are the declared
boundary of the system, fixed *before* the experiment starts. Everything
between them — belts, machine buffers, your pockets — is inside.
"Inside" and "outside" are decided by the declaration, not by what feels
like part of the factory.

This is what makes counting exact. Admissions are crossings of one
declared surface; completions are crossings of another; WIP is what has
crossed the first and not the second. Move the boundary and all three
numbers legitimately change — which is why FISL freezes it into the
scenario's identity, and why comparing runs is only meaningful when that
identity is the same.

## Windows: half-open, tick-exact

The experiment clock is the simulation's own tick counter — not wall
time, not your watch. A measurement window is a **half-open interval**
of ticks, $[a, b)$: it owns its first tick and does not own its last.

![Adjacent windows tile the clock exactly. The boundary tick belongs to
the window that starts on it — never to both, never to
neither.](../images/interludes/windows.svg){width=100%}

The payoff is boring and absolute: adjacent windows tile time with no
gap and no overlap, so an event is counted exactly once no matter how
phases are cut. Warmup, measured window, and any tail phases are all
intervals of this kind. When you later see a number that depends
delicately on its window — and in Lab 6 you will meet one that hides for
twelve minutes — the window convention is what lets you reason about it
instead of shrugging.

## Conservation is the auditor

The WIP number is bookkeeping: admissions minus completions, maintained
as a ledger. Bookkeeping can drift from reality, so FISL periodically
takes a **census** — physically counting every workpiece in the zone,
your inventory included — and demands the ledger and the census agree
*exactly*, with zero tolerance. Disagreement doesn't adjust the number;
it flags the run.

That last clause is the rule of evidence in miniature: **a measurement
problem is reported, never repaired silently.** A run can complete and
still carry validity flags; the flags travel with every number derived
from it. You will never be handed a cleaned-up figure with the cleaning
hidden.

## Reproducibility is the apparatus

The simulation is deterministic and every rate in it is a constant.
Rerun a scenario without intervening and you get — not approximately,
*bit-for-bit* — the same telemetry and the same report. This is what
makes your runs experiments in the scientific sense: an intervention's
effect is the entire difference between two runs, with nothing left over
for luck to explain. It is a luxury no real factory offers, and the
course spends it deliberately: every disagreement between your
prediction and the data is a wrong prediction, never noise.

## Claims to carry into Lab 1

Lab 1 puts two machines in series, and their catalog capacities differ:
the first can craft every 1.6 s, the second every 2.0 s. Before running:

1. Rerun any completed run without changing anything. Every reported
   number will repeat exactly — decimals and all. (Do this once; it is
   the cheapest calibration of trust you will ever perform.)
2. Over any window, the change in WIP will equal admissions minus
   completions in that window, exactly. The census guarantees you'd be
   told otherwise.
3. Convert the two craft times to capacities (60 s ÷ craft seconds) and
   write both down. The run will report *one* throughput. Predict which
   of your two numbers it is — and notice that you are already doing
   Lab 2's job.

## Further reading

- Hopp & Spearman, *Factory Physics* (3rd ed.), ch. 6 "A Science of
  Manufacturing" — the argument that manufacturing needs laws and
  measurements rather than slogans; this course's founding premise.
- P. J. Denning & J. P. Buzen, "The Operational Analysis of Queueing
  Network Models", *Computing Surveys* 10(3), 1978 — measurement laws
  stated as identities on observed data, exactly the stance FISL's
  ledger takes.
- The conventions here are FISL's ADRs 0001 (experiment time and
  phases), 0010 (observation windows), and 0017 (conservation-ledger WIP
  with census cross-check).
